title: PNAS | 中科大/武汉病毒研究所/昆明动物研究所在大别班达病毒治疗抗体研发上取得重要进展 - 搜狐网

analysis.time: Not reported in the supplied evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: China (Wuhan, Kunming) and Asian countries (Japan, Korea); human and animal hosts (mice, ferrets).
analysis.event: Confirmed: Researchers from Chinese Academy of Sciences Wuhan Institute of Virology, University of Science and Technology of China, and Kunming Institute of Zoology reported a bispecific antibody (N2D2-Fc-N2C1) that provides complete protection against SFTSV in mouse and ferret preclinical models.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Preclinical study showing 100% protection in mouse and ferret models; reduced viral load and clinical symptoms; no human case or death counts reported; risk not quantified.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: Confirmed research progress; preclinical testing in mouse and ferret models; no human trials yet; potential therapeutic candidate; further clinical evaluation required; source is news report of PNAS publication.

analysis.brief_en: Chinese researchers from the Chinese Academy of Sciences Wuhan Institute of Virology, University of Science and Technology of China, and Kunming Institute of Zoology have published a study in PNAS describing a new bispecific antibody, N2D2‐Fc‐N2C1, that fully protects mice and ferrets from severe fever with thrombocytopenia syndrome virus (SFTSV) in preclinical trials. The antibody, derived from two nanobodies targeting different regions of the virus’s Gn glycoprotein, neutralizes the virus by blocking attachment and fusion and acts synergistically. In IFNAR‐/‐ mouse models and a clinical‐grade aged ferret model, a low dose of 5 mg/kg given either preventively or one day after infection prevented disease and reduced viral load. The authors highlight the antibody’s advantage over conventional antibody cocktails, noting its single‐molecule format simplifies production and pharmacokinetics. While the results are promising, clinical trials are still needed to assess safety and efficacy in humans.
